title: A Well for the Visitor
premise: Rafael Eriksen, a property surveyor estranged from his own past, is sent to appraise the Holloway farmhouse and discovers it is a counting house: every generation, something in the well beneath it counts the family down to zero. The 'imaginary friend' from Rafael's childhood — a boy called Wren who never aged — is the house's herald, and Rafael was meant to be counted fifteen years ago but escaped by being forgotten. Now the Holloways' youngest daughter can see Wren too, and as the count accelerates, Rafael must choose between fleeing again or becoming the house's final number so the family he's come to love can belong to each other instead of to the well.
about_author: Ada Lockridge is the pen name of a former rural assessor who spent a decade inspecting abandoned properties across the upper Midwest before turning to horror. She writes about houses that remember their occupants better than the occupants remember themselves.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Rafael arrives at the Holloway farmhouse for a routine estate appraisal, noting off measurements — rooms that don't sum, a well cap bolted from inside. He hears a familiar knock-pattern in the walls and tells himself it's settling. Beat: professional detachment beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. At dusk he finds a boy of about eight sitting on the porch rail, unchanged after fifteen years: Wren, the friend only Rafael ever saw. Wren says simply, 'You're late.' Rafael flees to his truck; the engine turns over but the road behind him loops back to the house. Beat: dread made intimate.

chapters.title: The Holloways
chapters.summary: POV Marisol Holloway. Marisol, widowed mother of three, interviews the shaken surveyor and offers him lodging when his car dies. Her youngest, Birdie, mentions 'the counting boy' at dinner, and the table goes silent. Beat: warmth established inside something already wrong.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Unable to leave, Rafael catalogs the house's anomalies with surveyor's precision — doors that gain hinges, a staircase one step longer each night. Flashbacks reveal how young Rafael stopped seeing Wren after promising to forget him. Beat: the cost of denial named.

chapters.title: The Well Cap
chapters.summary: POV Birdie. Seven-year-old Birdie follows knocking sounds to the cellar and finds the iron well cap warm, ticking like a clock. She counts the ticks aloud and the house seems to listen. Beat: innocence touching the mechanism.

chapters.title: What Wren Counts
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Wren appears inside the locked house and explains the rules without cruelty: the house keeps a family until the count finishes; the count is people. Rafael realizes the previous owners' names on the deed all end the same year. Beat: rules of the horror clarified.

chapters.title: Marisol's Inheritance
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Going through her late husband's papers, Marisol finds letters showing he knew — payments to a 'surveyor' dating back decades, and a note: 'It only needs one who remembers.' She begins to suspect Rafael is why the house woke. Beat: trust fraying.

chapters.title: Birdie's Friend
chapters.summary: POV Birdie. Birdie plays with Wren happily; he teaches her counting games that make the walls hum approval. Rafael catches them and panics, but Birdie defends Wren fiercely. Beat: the horror wearing a beloved face.

chapters.title: The Road That Loops
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Rafael attempts to drive the family out; the county roads fold back on themselves no matter the direction. Cell service shows calls placed years ago. They return to find the porch light already on for them. Beat: escape closed off; siege begins.

chapters.title: One Step Longer
chapters.summary: POV Theo, seventeen. The eldest son maps the house nightly and proves it's growing — square footage accruing like interest. He becomes obsessed, measuring obsessively, sleeping in the addition that shouldn't exist. Beat: power of the house seducing a mind.

chapters.title: The Previous Tenant
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. In the attic Rafael finds a journal from 1974 by a man who tried to substitute himself for his family — and failed, because the house requires a willing memory, not just a body. The journal's last page bears Rafael's childhood handwriting. Beat: revelation deepens the trap.

chapters.title: What Rafael Forgot
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Under hypnosis-like recall triggered by the cellar, Rafael remembers: he lived here as a foster child; the Holloways' predecessor family took him in; Wren saved him by making the house forget him, breaking the count. His debt is fifteen years old. Beat: identity overturned.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Marisol confronts Rafael, then offers herself to the house to spare the children — and the walls go quiet, pleased. Rafael realizes her sacrifice will only reset the count, not end it. Beat: love weaponized against them.

chapters.title: Theo's Addition
chapters.summary: POV Theo. Theo, half-claimed by the growing wing of the house, refuses to leave his measurements; his shadow now moves a beat ahead of him. Rafael must physically drag him back across the threshold. Beat: corruption of power shown in one person.

chapters.title: Counting Down
chapters.summary: POV Birdie. The ticks under the floor speed up. Birdie, who understands the games best, tells Rafael the count is at four: 'Mama, Theo, you, me.' She isn't afraid; she's furious. Beat: the smallest voice states the stakes.

chapters.title: Wren's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Wren admits he was the first counted child, centuries ago, hollowed into a herald; he saved Rafael hoping Rafael would come back and finish what he couldn't — unmake the well. But unmaking requires someone the house has already counted. Beat: hope with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: The Night of Three
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. The count reaches three as the house seals itself: windows become walls, the front door opens onto the cellar. The family shelters together in one room, telling stories to stay whole. Beat: found family crystallizing under pressure.

chapters.title: Two
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Theo is taken into the walls — not dead, but kept, his voice joining the knocking. Rafael, next in the count, descends to the well cap while Marisol holds Birdie above. Beat: descent, resolve hardening into acceptance.

chapters.title: One
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. At the well, Rafael offers the thing below his remembered name — the one currency it cannot take by force. Wren stands beside him, and for the first time in centuries, the herald chooses: he steps into the count in Rafael's place, whispering 'You were never late. You came back.' Beat: sacrifice reframed as friendship repaid.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: POV Birdie. The count completes; the well exhales; the house stops growing and begins, slowly, to shrink — releasing Theo, cold but alive, and letting the roads run straight again. Birdie counts nothing at all and likes the sound of it. Beat: release.

chapters.title: Appraised Fair
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Weeks later, the Holloways sign papers selling the house to a land trust; the new surveyor finds nothing unusual except a well filled with clean earth. Marisol asks Rafael — no longer a stranger — to stay for dinner, permanently. Beat: belonging chosen, not assigned.

chapters.title: A Boy on No Porch
chapters.summary: POV Rafael, epilogue. Driving away from a routine job months later, Rafael passes an empty farmhouse and sees, briefly, a boy on the rail — older now, maybe ten, waving goodbye rather than waiting. Rafael waves back and does not stop. Beat: grief and gratitude braided; the door left ajar.
